modules.trigger: Establish a Term Loan / debt recycling (GEARING)
modules.scopeGate: Only if a gearing strategy is scoped

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you establish a Term Loan for investment purposes using your existing home or investment property loan as equity.We recommend you utilise the offset account against your home mortgage.
soa.outcomesLine: A debt recycling strategy essentially converts your non tax deductible (home loan) debt into tax deductible investment debt over a period of time.
why: Many people wait until their home loan is repaid before starting to invest. A strategy that lets you invest now and continue to pay off your home loan reasonably quickly is called debt recycling. It involves three key steps: use your home equity as security for a separate investment loan; use any tax savings (and surplus cash flow) to reduce your outstanding home loan balance; re‑borrow from your investment loan the amount you have paid off your home loan to purchase additional investments.
Refinance of your existing loan structure to use available equity will allow you to begin investing more now as opposed to waiting until the loan is fully repaid.
Replaces “bad” (non tax deductible) debt with “good” (tax deductible) investment debt.
Allows for your home loan to be repaid in approximately XX years instead of XX years.
Allows you to utilise your Term Loan to invest in assets sooner than would have otherwise been possible.

Additional Benefits: Interest on investment debt provides ongoing tax deductions, reducing the amount of interest you pay. Debt recycling helps to establish an investment portfolio sooner and allows a portfolio to realise long term growth.
risks: You remain liable for the principal borrowed, irrespective of the performance of your investment portfolio;
There is the risk of the lender having recourse to the home used as security, and therefore the risk of losing the home;

If interest rates increase your interest payments will increase accordingly, requiring additional cash. Gearing increases the risk attached to a portfolio, as gearing will magnify both gains and losses;
Gearing is inappropriate for people without satisfactory cash flow/income to meet borrowing costs;
While gearing enhances your potential for bigger gains, it can also expose you to a greater risk in a falling market;
Assets purchased with borrowed funds may actually fall in value. This means that although you might receive extra tax deductions over time, you might actually lose funds;
Due to the high risk nature of a gearing strategy, I recommend that you review the suitability of your leveraged portfolio on at least an annual basis;

A gearing strategy requires a long term investment horizon. Investment returns can be volatile, and in order to withstand short term fluctuations, I recommend a minimum 5 year investment time horizon;
alternatives: We considered restructuring all of your lending to interest only loans and making additional salary sacrifice contributions to super for the difference you were paying on your home loan principal. I have discounted this strategy because home ownership is a higher priority for you than growing your superannuation at this time and you wish to take advantage of a debt recycling strategy to reduce your “bad” non tax deductible debt within your existing loan account and pay your home off as soon as possible.

risks: A joint account exposes the full balance to either party's creditors and is treated as a shared asset on separation.
Income and capital gains are split per ownership, which may not be the most tax-effective split if your incomes differ materially.
alternatives: Hold separate individual accounts (cleaner separation) or invest in the lower-income earner's name (more tax-effective) — chosen approach reflects your preference for a shared plan.

modules.trigger: Reserves & cash buffer for tactical liquidity (avoid forced selling)
modules.scopeGate: Investment / pension portfolio where a cash/reserves sleeve is held

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you set aside funds in Reserves & Cash to provide you with liquidity and low volatility, so you shouldn't have to sell growth assets through necessity or bad decisions during downturns.
soa.outcomesLine: A reserves sleeve funds your needs through market falls, so growth assets are not sold at the wrong time.
why: Holding a low-volatility reserve protects you from forced sales at market troughs and preserves your growth assets to recover.
You rebalance by topping up reserves from growth assets as part of your annual review.

The reserve can be phased to your circumstances — e.g. hold a reduced reserve (1.5 years instead of the usual 2.5 years of pension requirements) where known cash inflows such as upcoming property sales are due, then restore it, reviewed each year.
risks: Holding reserves creates a return drag during strong markets; the allocation must be rebalanced to stay aligned with your risk profile.
alternatives: Remain fully invested for higher expected return — discounted as it exposes you to forced selling in downturns.

risks: Selling existing holdings to rebalance may crystallise CGT and incur transaction costs.

why: Avoids capital gains and transaction costs of switching where the existing platform/option remains suitable.
risks: The existing platform may cost more than alternatives; reviewed at each ongoing review.

modules.trigger: Money on the move (MOTM) framework

soa.strategiesLine: As per the Money on the Move framework, for every 5% drop in the market we may bring forward 1 month's Dollar Cost Averaging to ensure your funds are invested as efficiently as possible. The above initial and ongoing DCA investment amounts will also be subject to change based on current market valuations and our Money on the Move framework to ensure your funds are invested as effectively as possible.
soa.outcomesLine: Your funds will be invested efficiently, with dollar cost averaging accelerated when markets fall to take advantage of lower entry prices.
why: The Money on the Move framework accelerates your dollar cost averaging when markets fall, allowing you to take advantage of lower entry prices while maintaining the discipline of a staged investment approach.
risks: Accelerating investment into falling markets means more of your capital is exposed if markets continue to decline before recovering.
Market timing adjustments are made at the manager's discretion and outcomes may differ from a fixed dollar-cost-averaging schedule.
alternatives: We considered a fixed dollar-cost-averaging schedule without the Money on the Move overlay. This was not recommended as it does not take advantage of lower entry prices when markets fall.

modules.trigger: Add a reserves portfolio

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend the inclusion of the Reserves Portfolio to provide a source of liquidity to fund pension payments and short-term income needs. This may assist in reducing the need to draw on growth assets during periods of market volatility, thereby helping to manage sequencing risk.
soa.outcomesLine: A Reserves Portfolio provides liquidity for your income needs and reduces the need to sell growth assets during market downturns.
why: The Reserves Portfolio provides a dedicated source of liquidity so that pension payments and short-term income needs can be met without selling growth assets at depressed prices.
Separating reserves from growth assets helps manage sequencing risk — the risk of poor returns early in retirement permanently reducing your capital.
risks: Funds held in the Reserves Portfolio are invested defensively and are expected to earn lower long-term returns than growth assets.
In a prolonged market downturn the reserves may be exhausted, requiring you to draw funds when markets are down.
alternatives: We considered holding your entire portfolio in growth assets without a reserves allocation. This was not recommended as markets falling early in your drawdown phase could force the sale of growth assets at depressed prices, permanently reducing your capital.

modules.trigger: Commence drawdown (draw an income from the investment)
triggerPhrases: draw an income from the investment

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you commence a drawdown of $___ from your investment account to help meet your income needs. Drawing an income stream will provide you with the funds required to maintain your lifestyle in line with your financial freedom goals.
soa.outcomesLine: Your investment drawdown will provide the income required to maintain your lifestyle in line with your financial freedom goals.
why: Drawing an income from your investment account provides the funds required to maintain your lifestyle in line with your financial freedom goals.
Funding your lifestyle in this manner draws down your capital in a structured, tax-aware manner while the balance remains invested.
risks: Regular drawdowns reduce your invested capital, and if drawdowns exceed investment returns your balance will decline over time.
Poor market returns early in the drawdown phase (sequencing risk) may reduce how long your funds will last — this may require you to draw funds when markets are down.
alternatives: We considered funding your income needs from cash savings alone. This was not recommended as it would exhaust your liquid reserves and forgo the tax-effective, structured drawdown available from your investment account.

modules.trigger: DCA strategy — % upfront, remainder dollar cost averaged over 12 months

soa.strategiesLine: ___% of your funds will be lump sum invested & the remainder will be Dollar Cost Averaged over 12 months.
soa.outcomesLine: Your funds will be progressively invested over 12 months, reducing the impact of short-term market volatility on your entry prices.
why: Staging your investment through dollar cost averaging reduces the risk of investing your entire balance immediately before a market fall, while ensuring your funds are progressively invested in line with your risk profile.
risks: If markets rise during the averaging period, the staged portion of your funds will buy in at higher prices than an immediate lump-sum investment.
Funds awaiting investment earn cash returns only and will not participate in market growth until invested.
alternatives: We considered investing 100% of your funds immediately. This was not recommended as a significant market fall shortly after investment would have an outsized impact on your capital.

modules.trigger: 100% lump sum invested

soa.strategiesLine: 100% of your funds will be lump sum invested upon implementation.
soa.outcomesLine: Your funds will be fully invested from implementation, maximising your time in the market.
why: Investing the full amount immediately maximises your time in the market, which historically has been more reliable than attempting to time entry points for amounts of this size.
risks: A significant market fall shortly after implementation would affect your full invested balance.
You will experience market volatility from the outset.
alternatives: We considered dollar cost averaging your funds into the market over 12 months. This was not recommended for your circumstances as staging the investment would leave funds in cash earning lower returns, and time in the market is expected to outweigh timing the market.

modules.trigger: In-specie transfer to minimise buy/sell spread & time out of market risks

soa.strategiesLine: An in-specie transfer reduces the need to sell down assets, withdraw funds to your bank account, or re-purchase assets. This transfer process saves you on associated transaction costs and buy/sell spreads, and minimises out of market risks, ensuring your portfolios remain invested.
soa.outcomesLine: Your holdings transfer in-specie, saving transaction costs and buy/sell spreads and keeping your portfolio invested throughout.
why: Transferring your holdings in-specie keeps your portfolio invested throughout the transfer, avoiding time-out-of-market risk.
Avoiding the sell-down and re-purchase saves transaction costs and buy/sell spreads, and avoids unnecessarily crystallising capital gains.
risks: Not all holdings may be transferable in-specie — any residual assets may need to be sold and transferred as cash, with associated costs and CGT implications.
The transfer process may take time to complete, during which changes to the portfolio cannot be made.
alternatives: We considered selling your holdings and transferring the proceeds as cash. This was not recommended as it would incur transaction costs and buy/sell spreads, potentially crystallise capital gains, and leave your funds out of the market during the transfer.

modules.trigger: Establish new fund + full rollover (close & transfer 100%)
triggerPhrases: rollover full benefits to new fund

soa.strategiesLine: [Name], we recommend you close your existing [Fund] and transfer 100% of the balance to a new fund that has been customised for your needs.[Name], we recommend that you provide your employer with the details of your new superannuation fund to ensure all future contributions are directed to your new account.
soa.outcomesLine: Your superannuation strategies will be professionally managed in a way to maximise your superannuation benefits and stay in line with your needs. We estimate your new fund to have a total balance of approximately $XXX in XX years' time.
why: Your superannuation will be invested in line with your risk profile and will help you achieve your goal of maximising your superannuation for retirement while being managed on your behalf.
Increased investment choice, which provides your adviser with the ability to tailor your investment portfolio to your long term investment strategy.
Achieve your goal of partially funding adviser fees from superannuation and the ability to maintain ongoing advice.

Seamless transfer from accumulation to pension (not required to sell down your assets to transfer into the pension phase). This can prevent unnecessary Capital Gains Tax consequences and/or sale of assets at a time of unfavourable market conditions.
risks: Generally, any money held within superannuation is not accessible until retirement.
Depending on the components that make up your superannuation benefits, withdrawing money before age 60 may result in lump sum tax being payable.
When you die, the proceeds from your superannuation fund may be subject to lump sum tax if paid to non-dependants.
There may be transaction costs involved in establishing the strategy.
alternatives: Rollover part of your super in order to retain your existing insurance cover within super. I have discounted this strategy as the recommended replacement insurance cover provides additional benefits (such as improved definitions and access to trauma insurance)... a partial rollover would also mean more than one super account, which makes keeping track of your super more difficult.
Retain your existing super accounts. I discounted this strategy as your existing super account has limited functionality for your adviser to easily manage your superannuation on your behalf.

modules.trigger: Establish new fund + partial rollover, retain minimum for insurance

soa.strategiesLine:
[Name], we recommend you retain the minimum required ($XXX) in your existing [Fund] to retain your underwritten [Life & TPD] insurance and transfer the remaining balance to a new fund that has been customised for your needs.
	[Name], we recommend that you continue to direct your super guarantee to your existing [Fund] account and we recommend making annual partial rollovers to your new fund.
soa.outcomesLine: Retaining your existing fund allows you to keep your underwritten insurance cover while moving the balance to a professionally managed fund.
risks: By maintaining two superannuation accounts you will incur a duplication of fees and increased administration effort to maintain your multiple accounts.
You will experience market volatility. There may be transaction costs involved in establishing the strategy.
Withdrawing money from superannuation as a lump sum before you reach age 60 may result in lump sum tax being payable.
Do not cancel the old fund's cover until the new cover is confirmed in place — if the new application is declined or modified, the old cover cannot be reinstated.
alternatives: We considered closing your existing super accounts and rolling over 100% of the balance to a new fund, however we discounted this strategy in order to maintain your insurance cover held within your existing super account.

modules.trigger: Retain existing fund (invest in line with risk profile)
triggerPhrases: retain and invest in line with risk profile

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you retain your existing [Fund] Superannuation account (in line with your risk profile) that has been customised for your needs. We recommend that you continue to direct your employer contributions to your existing [Fund] account.
soa.outcomesLine: Your superannuation will be invested in line with your risk profile and will help you achieve your goal of maximising your superannuation for retirement.
why: Increased investment choice, which provides your adviser with the ability to tailor your investment portfolio to your long term investment strategy.
You can fund your insurance premiums through your superannuation account as desired.
Reinvesting distributions will accelerate the growth potential and the benefits from compounding growth.
Retained to minimise crystallising capital gains tax on existing holdings.
risks: Generally, any money held within superannuation is not accessible until retirement.
The underlying investments within super involve investment risk and do not guarantee your returns; values may fall.
alternatives: An alternative is investing using a passive index fund approach instead of an actively managed approach like CARE. We have discounted this strategy as we believe the actively managed asset mix offered through CARE provides the optimal way to achieve your long term investment goals while minimising volatility over the short term.

modules.trigger: Consolidate multiple super accounts

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you consolidate your existing superannuation accounts into a single fund customised for your needs (after confirming no valuable insurance or benefits are lost).
soa.outcomesLine: Consolidating your super reduces duplicated fees and simplifies the management of your retirement savings.
why: Avoid multiple sets of fees – one fund means one set of fees.
Keep better track of your superannuation investment when it's in one place.
By having all of your super together in one account it's easier to plan for a future that includes a comfortable retirement.
risks: Having a number of superannuation plans results in additional fees, difficulty keeping track of your funds and difficulty in maintaining a suitable investment strategy — however you may lose insurance cover or benefits held in a fund being closed, so confirm before consolidating.
alternatives: Retain separate accounts — discounted where duplicated fees and administration outweigh any benefit of multiple funds.

modules.trigger: In-specie transfer of super holdings

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend completing an in-specie transfer of your [SMSF / existing] assets ([Hub24 Investment and MCMA]) into a personal superannuation fund tailored to your needs.
soa.outcomesLine: An in-specie transfer keeps your portfolio invested while moving it to the recommended fund, saving transaction costs and buy/sell spreads and minimising out-of-market risk.
why: An in-specie transfer reduces the need to sell down assets, withdraw funds to your bank account, or re-purchase assets. This saves you on associated transaction costs and buy/sell spreads, and minimises out-of-market risk, ensuring your portfolios remain invested.

The recommended platform (Hub24) offers the option to in-specie transfer eligible investment options, helping you consolidate your investments into a single platform and streamline ongoing management and administration.
risks: Assets that are not eligible for in-specie transfer (or that cannot be internally netted) may need to be sold down, which may crystallise capital gains tax — consult your accountant.

modules.trigger: Retain a defined benefit fund (scope out)

soa.strategiesLine: [Name], we recommend you retain your existing Defined Benefit [Fund] account including the insurance arrangements held within this account. [Name], your employer superannuation contributions are required to continue to be directed to your existing defined benefit account while you remain employed in the [public sector].
soa.outcomesLine: Retaining your defined benefit account preserves your guaranteed scheme benefits and existing insurance.
why: Preserves the guaranteed/defined-benefit entitlement and any valuable insurance held in the scheme.
Where the DB fund provides inbuilt Life and Income Protection benefits, these are retained as there is no premium cost charged to you for these benefits.
risks: Due to restrictions within the fund (Defined Benefit portion) — and because the benefit is determined by a formula — we are unable to make any changes or provide advice on this; it is scoped out.
Defined benefit entitlements are subject to specific scheme rules, preservation requirements and legislative considerations which differ from accumulation funds.
alternatives: Transfer the balance to an accumulation fund — discounted as it would forgo the valuable defined‑benefit entitlement.

modules.trigger: Retain military super (member & ancillary + employer/DB portion)

soa.strategiesLine: [Name], we recommend you retain your existing Military Super, including the insurance arrangements held within this account, while you remain in service. We have scoped out your Military Super (Defined Benefit portion) from this advice.
soa.outcomesLine: Retaining your military super preserves the employer/defined‑benefit entitlement and any insurance, while we manage the balance of your strategy.
why: Preserves the employer/defined-benefit entitlement and any valuable insurance held in the scheme.
risks: You are required to retain the defined benefit portion in your existing Military Super fund (Employer Benefit portion) as you are unable to access this until age 55 — it is scoped out of this advice.
These funds are not accessible until a condition of release is met, nor can they be rolled over to another fund.
alternatives: Roll the member & ancillary balance to an accumulation fund — the employer/defined-benefit portion must be retained while in service.

modules.trigger: Redirect / continue employer contributions

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend that you provide your employer with the details of your new superannuation fund to ensure all future contributions are directed to your new account.(OR, where a fund is retained:) We recommend that you continue to direct your employer contributions to your existing [Fund].
soa.outcomesLine: Ensures your employer contributions flow to the appropriate fund under the recommended strategy.
why: Keeps future contributions aligned with the recommended fund structure.

modules.trigger: Establish / set up an SMSF (and manage — rebalance + pension transition)

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you establish a new Account Based Pension account and invest in line with your risk profile.We recommend you commence drawing an income of $XXX p.a. through your Account Based Pension account.
soa.outcomesLine: We estimate your funds will sustain your desired income, making you able to draw approximately $XXX p.a. for approximately XX years.
why: Rolling over the accumulation portion to a pension account will mean all future earnings within this fund will be tax free.
Drawing an income stream will provide you with the funds required to maintain your lifestyle in line with your retirement goals.
Funding your lifestyle in this manner will ensure you're drawing down your retirement capital in the most tax efficient manner.
risks: Generally, any money held within superannuation is not accessible until retirement.
When you die, the proceeds from your superannuation fund may be subject to tax if they are paid as a lump sum to non-dependants, as defined for tax purposes.
The underlying investments within super involve some investment risk and do not guarantee your returns; values may fall.
Amounts moved to pension phase count toward your transfer balance cap; minimum annual pension payments must be drawn.
alternatives: Remain in accumulation phase / take a partial rollover — if a partial rollover were to take place, this would also mean you end up with more than one super account, which makes keeping track of your super more difficult over time.

modules.trigger: Commence a pension / transition to retirement (TTR)

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you establish a new Transition to Retirement (TTR) pension account through your existing [Hub24 Super] platform and invest in line with your risk profile using the CARE Philosophy.We recommend you roll over the full balance from your existing [Fund] (Accumulation) account into your new TTR pension account.We recommend you withdraw the maximum allowable 10% of your TTR account balance as a lump sum each financial year — approximately $XXX per annum.
soa.outcomesLine: Investment earnings within a TTR account are tax-free, and as you are over age 60 all income payments from the TTR pension are also tax-free, supplementing your cashflow while you remain employed.
why: Your superannuation will be invested in line with your risk profile and will help you achieve your goal of maximising your superannuation for retirement while being managed on your behalf.
Investment earnings within a TTR account are tax-free, and as you are over age 60, all income payments received from the TTR pension will also be tax-free.
Drawing an income stream will provide you with the funds required to support your cashflow requirements.
risks: A TTR strategy is primarily designed to supplement your income while you remain employed. It should be reviewed annually to ensure it continues to meet your income needs, remains aligned with your retirement objectives, and reflects any future legislative changes affecting TTR pension rules.
Withdrawing funds now will reduce the amount available when you convert your TTR pension to a full retirement pension.
There is the normal risk of markets falling and unforeseen circumstances requiring you to draw funds when markets are down.
alternatives: We considered rolling over your full [existing] super account and rolling over 100% of the balance to the existing [Hub24] Super fund, however we discounted this strategy in order to maintain your insurance cover held within your existing super account.

modules.trigger: Recontribution strategy

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you establish two new superannuation accounts and invest in line with your risk profile. We recommend you make a non-concessional contribution of $XXX into [Account 2] to facilitate the implementation of a recontribution strategy.
soa.outcomesLine: A recontribution strategy converts a taxable component into a tax-free component, improving the tax treatment of your super death benefit for non-dependant beneficiaries.
why: Converts a taxable component to a tax-free component. A super death benefit paid to a dependant is tax free; if paid to a non-dependant, the tax payable depends on the components that make up the benefit — increasing the tax-free proportion reduces potential death benefits tax.
Can be combined with spouse equalisation to make better use of both transfer balance caps.
risks: You must have met a condition of release to withdraw; the recontribution counts toward your non-concessional cap and is preserved. Obtain advice on the tax components before implementing.
alternatives: Retain the existing components — discounted where improving the tax-free proportion benefits your beneficiaries.

modules.trigger: SMSF wind-up / split on separation (in-specie to personal super)

soa.strategiesLine: Following your separation, we recommend completing an in-specie transfer of your allocated SMSF assets into a personal superannuation fund tailored to your needs.
soa.outcomesLine: Moving your allocated SMSF assets in-specie to a personal fund keeps them invested while removing the ongoing trustee obligations of the SMSF following separation.
why: Keeps your share of the assets invested while transferring them out of the SMSF, avoiding sell-down costs and out-of-market risk.
Removes the ongoing administration, audit and trustee compliance obligations of maintaining the SMSF after separation.
risks: Assets not eligible for in-specie transfer may need to be sold down, which may crystallise CGT.
SMSF wind-up has its own administrative and compliance steps; consult your accountant/SMSF administrator.
alternatives: Retain the SMSF — discounted where, following separation, the cost and complexity of the SMSF is no longer appropriate.

modules.trigger: Disability super benefit — staged lump-sum withdrawals (TPD/disability payout, tax-free uplift)
modules.scopeGate: Client has met a disability/permanent-incapacity condition of release; super boosted by a TPD/disability insurance payout
modules.figures: Staged one-off withdrawal amounts; tax-free vs taxable %; 22% tax withheld

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you make one-off lump sum withdrawals from your new Accumulation fund as a disability super benefit (e.g. $80,550 in FY25/26, $40,000 in FY26/27, $15,000 in FY27/28) to fund your planned expenses, alongside commencing a pension income to cover your cashflow shortfall.
soa.outcomesLine: At the time of writing, it is estimated that your balance after uplift will comprise approximately 48% tax-free and 52% taxable components.
why: Because you have met a permanent-incapacity condition of release, you can access your superannuation as a disability super benefit, which receives a tax-free component uplift (the tax-free proportion is increased to reflect your prospective service period to retirement).
Staged lump-sum withdrawals fund known upcoming expenses while keeping the balance invested in line with your risk profile.
risks: The 22% tax will be withheld at the time of each withdrawal. You are likely to receive a refund for the excess tax withheld when you lodge your tax return — consult an accountant before implementing.

As these withdrawals are intended for immediate expenses, no adverse impact on your Disability Support Pension (DSP) is expected under the assets and income test. However, if the withdrawn funds are not spent and remain in your savings account, your DSP payments may temporarily reduce until your balance falls below the relevant threshold.
The projection does not account for additional ad hoc withdrawals or material increases in pension drawdowns; we review annually.
alternatives: Draw all income via pension only — discounted as it does not provide the lump sums needed for your planned one-off expenses.

modules.trigger: Reversionary beneficiary nomination (pension phase)

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you nominate a reversionary beneficiary within your recommended pension funds. A reversionary nomination allows the nominated dependant to automatically receive the pension payments in the event of your passing.
soa.outcomesLine: Seamless continuation of pension income to your surviving spouse, avoiding a lump-sum death benefit and probate delay.
why: The pension automatically continues to your nominated dependant on death, preserving the tax-effective income stream.
Death benefit payment option — you can nominate dependants under the non-lapsing binding election, or you can select an automatic reversionary pension under the pension plan.
risks: A reversionary nomination is generally only available to a spouse/de facto; it reduces flexibility if the beneficiary's circumstances change (a new nomination is required).
If the reversionary beneficiary pre-deceases you, the benefit reverts to your estate unless a backup nomination is in place.
alternatives: Non-lapsing binding death benefit nomination only — provides a lump sum rather than a continuing income stream; less seamless for a surviving spouse in pension phase.

modules.trigger: Seamless accumulation-to-pension transfer (no asset sale; avoid CGT / poor-timing sale)
modules.scopeGate: Commencing an account-based pension from an existing accumulation account on the same platform

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend a seamless transfer from accumulation to pension — you are not required to sell down your assets to transfer into the pension phase.
soa.outcomesLine: Your assets move into the tax-free pension environment without being sold, preserving your position.
why: This can prevent unnecessary Capital Gains Tax consequences and/or sale of assets at a time of unfavourable market conditions.
It maintains your existing investment holdings and their long-term timing.
risks: Some platforms charge for in-specie transfers; holdings remain subject to market movements in the pension phase.
alternatives: Sell down in accumulation and re-buy in pension — discounted as it can crystallise CGT and forces a sale that may occur at an unfavourable time.

modules.trigger: In-specie transfer of super on separation (SMSF asset split to personal super)
modules.scopeGate: Separation with an SMSF or jointly-held super to be split

soa.strategiesLine: Following your recent separation, we recommend completing an in-specie transfer of your allocated SMSF assets (e.g. the platform investment and cash account) into a personal superannuation fund tailored to your needs.
soa.outcomesLine: Your share of the fund moves to a personal super account without selling the underlying assets.
why: An in-specie transfer preserves your portfolio and avoids crystallising capital gains, buy/sell spreads and market-timing risk that a sell-down would create.
risks: There may be transaction costs involved in establishing the strategy.
In-specie transfer may not be available for all asset types; the asset split documentation must be finalised before execution.
alternatives: Sell the SMSF assets and roll cash to personal super — discounted as it crystallises CGT and transaction costs.

modules.trigger: Commence pension before rebalancing to minimise CGT (defer rebalance to pension phase)
modules.scopeGate: SMSF/super moving to pension phase with a portfolio rebalance required

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend commencing pension phase prior to the rebalance, and deferring the rebalance of the portfolio until pension phase commences, to reduce the CGT impact on the portion of the balance transferred to retirement phase. Please consult your accountant to confirm the tax implications.
soa.outcomesLine: Assets are rebalanced once in the tax-free pension environment, reducing the capital gains tax on the changeover.
why: Selling to rebalance in accumulation phase can trigger CGT at 10–15%; deferring the rebalance until the assets support a retirement-phase income stream reduces or removes that tax.
Where the rebalance is done within the Account-Based Pension accounts, we do not anticipate it will crystallise a capital gain, so you should not incur CGT as a result of the rebalance.
On platforms that match buy and sell orders internally, the rebalance offsets purchases and sales and keeps your portfolio fully invested, avoiding time-out-of-market risk.

Where an SMSF asset (e.g. an investment property) is to be sold, commencing the Account-Based Pension before the sale means the fund is in retirement phase, so the sale is not expected to be subject to capital gains tax. Please consult your accountant to confirm prior to implementing.
risks: Markets may move while the rebalance is deferred; timing should be confirmed with your accountant.
alternatives: Rebalance immediately in accumulation phase — discounted as it crystallises avoidable CGT.

modules.trigger: Retain an existing SMSF (operate, add account, redirect contributions, reinvest)
modules.scopeGate: Existing SMSF that is to be kept (not wound up)

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you retain your existing SMSF. We recommend you establish a new investment account held by the SMSF (invested in line with your risk profile), retain your existing SMSF cash account, provide your employer with the fund details so future contributions are directed to the SMSF, and reinvest distributions from the SMSF investment portfolio.
soa.outcomesLine: Your SMSF continues as your super vehicle, with a customised investment account, a central cash account for transactions and compliance costs, all contributions consolidated to the fund, and distributions reinvested to compound.
why: Retaining the SMSF cash account consolidates all super transactions into one central account, easing monitoring and providing liquidity for ongoing costs and administrative fees of being an SMSF trustee.
Directing all future employer (and personal) contributions to the SMSF consolidates your super into one fund for easier management.
Reinvesting distributions accelerates growth potential through compounding.
risks: As trustee you remain responsible for the fund's compliance, administration and costs.
Reinvesting distributions means no access to that income until a condition of release is met.
alternatives: Wind up the SMSF and roll to a retail/platform fund — discounted where the SMSF holds assets (e.g. an investment property) central to your long-term strategy.

modules.trigger: SMSF with corporate trustee holding a geared investment property (LRBA cashflow)
modules.scopeGate: SMSF holding (or acquiring) real property, typically with secured debt

soa.strategiesLine: Your SMSF (corporate trustee — Pty Ltd ATF the fund) holds an investment property with secured debt. We recommend consolidating both members' existing super into the SMSF via full rollover, maintaining a dedicated cash reserve for SMSF administration and property-related costs, and deploying the property's net rental income to fund your ongoing regular SMSF contributions.
soa.outcomesLine: Both members' super is pooled in the SMSF behind the property, with a cash buffer for costs and rental surplus recycled into ongoing contributions.
why: A corporate trustee structure (Pty Ltd as trustee for the fund) simplifies succession and limits trustee liability compared with individual trustees.
Consolidating both members' balances and the rental surplus into the fund concentrates capital behind the long-term property strategy.
risks: SMSF borrowing and property holding add audit, compliance and liquidity complexity; the fund must hold enough cash to meet loan repayments and costs.
Property is illiquid and concentrated; a fall in value or rental income affects the fund's ability to meet obligations.
alternatives: Wind up the SMSF — discounted as the fund was established to hold the investment property as part of your long-term superannuation strategy.

modules.trigger: SMSF wind-up / consolidation to a retail fund (non-separation, cost/suitability driven)
modules.scopeGate: Existing SMSF whose original purpose no longer applies / costs outweigh benefit
modules.figures: Estimated reduction in ongoing admin fees p.a.

soa.strategiesLine: You have asked us to review the long-term suitability of retaining your SMSF. The initial purpose of establishing the SMSF was to purchase a property; as that is no longer being pursued, we recommend you close your SMSF and rollover the full benefits to a new retail/platform fund customised for your needs.
soa.outcomesLine: Your super is simplified into a retail/platform fund, removing the cost and trustee responsibilities of the SMSF while keeping access to the recommended investment portfolio.
why: We believe an SMSF is not the right vehicle for your super, considering your current SMSF position.
By simplifying your superannuation you will not be burdened by the responsibilities of operating an SMSF.
Since you are not actively considering purchasing property through your superannuation as initially planned, closing the SMSF aligns better with your current goals and objectives.
Transferring from an SMSF to a retail superannuation fund reduces your ongoing administrative fees and eliminates your legal and administrative responsibilities as an SMSF trustee.
We have discussed the short and long-term implications, including the costs that would occur if you ever wished to re-establish the SMSF in the future after winding it up now.
risks: The SMSF wind-up will require the sale of the existing share portfolio within the fund, which may have capital gains implications and transaction costs.
Wind-up costs include completion of the current and previous SMSF financial statements, tax returns and any audit/compliance costs.
alternatives: Retain your existing SMSF — discounted as an SMSF has high costs and ongoing legal/administrative trustee requirements that are not needed to meet your retirement goals where the original purpose is no longer being pursued.

modules.trigger: Establish new fund + partial rollover, retain minimum for higher SG contributions

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you retain the minimum balance in your existing fund to keep receiving your higher employer SG contributions, and roll the remainder to the new recommended fund.
why: Some employers pay a higher SG into the existing fund; retaining a minimum balance preserves that benefit while still consolidating the bulk of your super.
risks: Two accounts mean two sets of fees until the arrangement ends.

modules.trigger: Commence an Account-Based Pension and draw an income (minimum % or set amount)

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you commence an Account-Based Pension and draw [the minimum % / $___ p.a.] to meet your income needs / top up your pension / fund your financial-freedom goal.
why: Pension-phase earnings are tax-free and the income stream funds your retirement spending.
risks: Minimum drawdowns are mandatory and apply even in a market downturn.

modules.trigger: CGT implications on a super changeover (SMSF, or rebalance Vanguard↔CARE) (free text)

soa.strategiesLine: [Free-type the CGT implications of the super changeover — applies for SMSF or a rebalance between Vanguard and CARE; not required for a standard rollover. Consult accountant.]

modules.trigger: Phase a lump-sum super investment via money-on-the-move (DCA the rollover)

soa.strategiesLine: For the lump sum entering super, we recommend phasing it into the market via the money-on-the-move framework — bringing forward instalments as markets fall.
why: Phasing a large rollover smooths your entry price and reduces timing risk.

modules.trigger: Money on the move (MOTM) framework — phase the lump sum into super

soa.strategiesLine: As per the Money on the Move framework, for every 5% drop in the market we may bring forward 1 month's Dollar Cost Averaging to ensure your funds are invested as efficiently as possible.
soa.outcomesLine: Your super lump sum is phased into the market efficiently, accelerating when markets fall to take advantage of lower entry prices.
why: Phasing your superannuation lump sum under the Money on the Move framework accelerates investment when markets fall, taking advantage of lower entry prices while keeping the discipline of a staged approach.
risks: Accelerating investment into falling markets exposes more of your balance if markets continue to decline before recovering.
Outcomes may differ from a fixed dollar-cost-averaging schedule as adjustments are made based on market movements.
alternatives: We considered a fixed dollar-cost-averaging schedule for the rollover. This was not recommended as it does not take advantage of lower entry prices when markets fall.

modules.trigger: DCA strategy — % upfront, remainder dollar cost averaged over 12 months (super)

soa.strategiesLine: ___% of CARE funds will be lump sum invested upon rollover & the remainder will be Dollar Cost Averaged over 12 months.
soa.outcomesLine: Your rollover is progressively invested over 12 months, reducing the impact of short-term market volatility.
why: Staging the investment of your rollover through dollar cost averaging reduces the risk of investing the full balance immediately before a market fall.
risks: If markets rise during the averaging period, the staged portion will buy in at higher prices than an immediate investment.
Funds awaiting investment are held in cash within the fund and will not participate in market growth until invested.
alternatives: We considered investing 100% of the rollover immediately. This was not recommended as a significant market fall shortly after rollover would have an outsized impact on your retirement capital.

modules.trigger: 100% lump sum invested upon rollover

soa.strategiesLine: 100% of CARE funds will be lump sum invested upon rollover.
soa.outcomesLine: Your rollover is fully invested from implementation, maximising time in the market.
why: Investing the full rollover immediately maximises your time in the market, which is expected to outweigh attempting to time entry points.
risks: A significant market fall shortly after the rollover would affect your full balance.
You will experience market volatility from the outset.
alternatives: We considered dollar cost averaging the rollover into the market. This was not recommended for your circumstances as staged funds would sit in cash earning lower returns while awaiting investment.

modules.trigger: CGT applicable within super upon rollover or rebalance

soa.strategiesLine: It is anticipated that the rollover/rebalance will trigger a capital gains tax (CGT) event within your superannuation, resulting in tax being payable on some of the underlying holdings. Any available carried-forward capital losses may be used to offset these or future capital gains. We estimate an approximate CGT liability of $___.
soa.outcomesLine: You understand the anticipated CGT within super and it has been weighed against the benefits of the recommended changeover.
why: Disclosing the anticipated CGT impact ensures you understand the cost of the changeover before proceeding, and that it has been weighed against the benefits of the recommended strategy.
risks: The actual CGT payable may differ from the estimate depending on market values at the time of the transaction and the fund's tax position.
Assets held for less than 12 months will not be eligible for the CGT discount within the fund.
alternatives: We considered retaining the existing holdings to avoid the CGT event. This was not recommended as the long-term benefits of the recommended investment strategy are expected to outweigh the one-off tax cost.

modules.trigger: Apply for the Centrelink Age Pension (retirement trigger)

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend that next financial year, when you retire or reduce your work, you apply for the Centrelink Age Pension.
soa.outcomesLine: Your Age Pension entitlement supplements your retirement income and reduces the drawdown on your own capital.
why: An Age Pension entitlement supplements your retirement income and reduces the drawdown required from your own capital, helping your funds last longer.
Applying at the point your work reduces ensures you receive your entitlement from the earliest date you qualify.
risks: Age Pension entitlements are means-tested — changes to your assets, income or the means-test rules may reduce or remove your entitlement.
Processing can take time; applying late may forgo entitlements as payments are generally not backdated.
alternatives: We considered not applying and funding retirement entirely from your own capital. This was not recommended as it forgoes an entitlement that reduces the drawdown on your funds.

modules.trigger: Salary sacrifice / concessional contributions

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you [continue / increase / decrease / cease] your salary sacrifice (concessional) contributions of $___.
soa.outcomesLine: Making concessional contributions builds your retirement savings tax‑effectively and provides net tax savings of approximately $XXX p.a.
why: Save on income tax because your salary contributed into super is taxed at 15% (up to your concessional contributions cap), not your marginal tax rate, regardless of how much you earn.
Boost your super by contributing more now, creating a bigger nest egg for your retirement.

Suitable if you are under 75 and eligible to contribute, have a marginal tax rate above 15%, and can sacrifice income without a large impact on your lifestyle, with an employer willing to offer the arrangement.
Concessional contributions are taxed at 15% within super (up to your cap), not your marginal tax rate.
risks: Care should be taken to ensure your employee entitlements are not adversely impacted as a result of salary sacrificing, or that you don't breach your concessional contributions cap. Contributions are preserved until a condition of release is met.
alternatives: Invest the surplus outside super instead — discounted where the tax‑effectiveness of concessional contributions better meets the goal, noting reduced accessibility.

modules.trigger: Carry-forward (catch-up) concessional contributions

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you make a carry-forward concessional contribution of $XXX, utilising your unused concessional cap amounts from previous years (after the 15% contributions tax).
soa.outcomesLine: Using your carry‑forward concessional cap allows a larger tax‑deductible contribution this year, reducing your assessable income.
why: The carry-forward arrangements involve accessing unused concessional cap amounts from previous years. An unused cap amount occurs when the concessional contributions you made in a financial year were less than your general concessional contributions cap. You can use caps from up to five previous financial years.
Tax-effective: contributions are taxed at 15% rather than your marginal rate.
risks: To use your unused cap amounts: your total super balance at the end of 30 June of the previous financial year must be less than $500,000, and you must have made concessional contributions in the year that exceeded your general cap. Contributions are preserved until a condition of release is met.
alternatives: Contribute only up to the standard cap — discounted where the carry‑forward provides a greater tax benefit this year.

modules.trigger: Non-concessional contribution

soa.strategiesLine: This financial year, we recommend withdrawing [$amount] from your existing pension account and re-contributing it as a once-off non-concessional contribution as part of a re-contribution strategy. Next financial year, we recommend utilising the bring-forward rule to make a further non-concessional contribution of up to [$cap].
soa.outcomesLine: Increasing the tax-free proportion of your superannuation reduces potential tax payable on death benefits, particularly for non-tax-dependant beneficiaries such as your adult children.
why: Your existing pension comprises a taxable and a tax-free component. Withdrawing funds and re-contributing them as non-concessional contributions increases the tax-free proportion of your superannuation over time and improves overall tax efficiency.
It is expected to reduce potential tax payable on death benefits, particularly for non-tax-dependant beneficiaries such as adult children.
The strategy allows for optimal use of your available non-concessional contribution caps, including the bring-forward rule, to enhance long-term outcomes.
risks: There is a risk that you don't follow or stick with the strategy, particularly at market extremes.
If you don't communicate changes in your circumstances, goals and objectives to us, your portfolio may no longer be appropriate.
The underlying investments within super are invested in investment funds. This involves some investment risk and does not guarantee your returns — values may fall from time to time.
alternatives: Retain your existing pension account with current funds allocation. I discounted this strategy as the existing account has a high taxable component which makes your super less tax-effective as a wealth-transfer tool — compared to the tax-free component, it creates a larger tax liability for beneficiaries.

modules.trigger: Bring-forward non-concessional contribution

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you use the bring-forward rule to make a non-concessional contribution of $XXX (bringing forward up to three years of your non-concessional cap).
soa.outcomesLine: The bring‑forward rule lets you contribute a larger after‑tax amount now, accelerating your retirement savings.
why: The non-concessional cap is $120,000 for 2024/2025. If you are under 75 years of age during the financial year, a $360,000 contribution can be made by 'bringing forward' two years' worth of contribution caps (in addition to contributions from that year). Accelerates the build-up of retirement savings in the low-tax super environment.

The bring-forward non-concessional contribution can be funded from the proceeds of a property sale (e.g. $360,000 using a portion of the proceeds), moving sale proceeds into the tax-free/low-tax super environment across the three-year window.

The bring-forward rule lets you use future years' non-concessional caps to make a larger one-off contribution now, maximising the funds in the tax-free super environment to draw retirement income from.

The contribution can be made via in-specie transfer of an existing investment portfolio (rather than selling to cash and re-buying), saving transaction costs and buy/sell spreads and avoiding time out of the market — noting the in-specie transfer crystallises CGT on the transferred assets.
risks: Eligibility depends on your age and total super balance at the prior 30 June; contributions in excess of applicable limits will attract penalty tax. Triggering the bring-forward restricts contributions in the following years; contributions are preserved.
Sale proceeds must be held in cash until the contribution is made, which may mean time out of the market.
alternatives: Contribute within the standard annual cap — discounted where the larger up‑front contribution better meets the goal.

modules.trigger: Spouse contribution

soa.strategiesLine: [Name], we recommend you make an after-tax spouse contribution of up to $3,000 p.a. to [Spouse]'s super to boost their retirement savings and receive a tax offset.
soa.outcomesLine: A spouse contribution boosts your spouse's retirement savings and may provide you with a tax offset.
why: A spouse contribution involves making an after-tax contribution to a low-income earning spouse’s super fund to boost their retirement savings and receive a tax offset.
Under the current 2025/26 tax rules, you may be able to claim an 18% tax offset on super contributions up to $3,000 that you make on behalf of your non-working or lower-income-earner partner.

If your spouse receives $37,000 or less in the total of assessable income, fringe benefits and employer super contributions, then you can access the maximum tax offset of $540, provided an after-tax contribution of at least $3,000 is made.
risks: Contributions count toward your spouse's non-concessional cap; both must be Australian residents and not living separately and apart on a permanent basis; your spouse must be under 75.
alternatives: Contribute to your own super instead — discounted where equalising balances or the spouse offset better meets the goal.

modules.trigger: Government co-contribution

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you make a non-concessional (after-tax) contribution of up to $1,000 to superannuation to take advantage of the Federal Government co-contribution scheme.
soa.outcomesLine: A small after‑tax contribution can attract up to $500 from the Government, an immediate uplift to your super.
why: You receive a tax-free super contribution from the federal government when you make a non-concessional contribution to your super account, subject to you satisfying a work test, an income test and an age test.
If you earn $47,488 or less (for the 2025/2026 year), the federal government pays $0.50 (50 cents) for every dollar you contribute to your fund in after-tax dollars, up to a maximum of $500 a year.
risks: Eligibility depends on your income, age and total super balance; the contribution is preserved.
alternatives: Do not contribute — discounted as it forgoes the Government co‑contribution where you are eligible.

modules.trigger: Contribution splitting

soa.strategiesLine: [Name], we recommend you split up to 85% of your concessional (employer and personal tax-deductible) contributions of $XXX to [Spouse]'s super account.
soa.outcomesLine: Contribution splitting equalises your balances and can provide earlier access to super and a reduced tax liability.
why: Super contributions splitting generally allows you to split up to 85% of your employer super contributions and personal tax-deductible (concessional) contributions to your spouse's super account, so you can both maximise the benefits of super.
Splitting contributions to a spouse who will reach age 60 before you may allow you earlier access to your super monies and the tax-free status of super withdrawals for those aged 60 or over.
Suitable if you have a spouse eligible to receive super contributions, a spouse who will reach 60 before you, or you want to boost your spouse's super savings.
risks: Not all super funds offer contribution splitting. Super is subject to preservation rules and contributions cannot be accessed until a condition of release is met. When split to your spouse's account they do not count towards your spouse's concessional contributions cap (they count against yours).
alternatives: Retain the contributions in your own account — discounted where balance equalisation better meets the goal.

modules.trigger: Personal deductible contribution
triggerPhrases: claim a tax deduction for contribution

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you commence making yearly concessional (personal deductible) contributions, setting aside the funds in your cash account through the year and making the contribution as a lump sum each year, then claiming a tax deduction for it.
soa.outcomesLine: You use your concessional cap via a personal deductible contribution, reducing taxable income and building super, without needing a salary-sacrifice arrangement with your employer.
why: Making ongoing concessional contributions helps reduce the effect of adviser fees and insurance premiums on your superannuation balance.
Claiming the contribution as a tax deduction provides net tax savings by moving income into the 15% super environment instead of your marginal rate.
risks: You must stay within the concessional cap to avoid excess-contribution tax, and lodge a valid notice of intent to claim the deduction with your fund.
alternatives: Salary sacrifice via your employer — equivalent outcome but requires an employer arrangement; non-concessional contribution — discounted as it gives no deduction.

modules.trigger: Work test note (age 67+)

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend ensuring contributions are made prior to turning age 67, due to potential work test requirements and contribution eligibility restrictions.
why: Prior to age 67, a person can make superannuation contributions without restriction. Between 67 and 74, tax deduction claims can only be made if the work test is satisfied (gainfully employed at least 40 hours over not more than 30 consecutive days in the financial year).

modules.trigger: Downsizer contribution

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you utilise the downsizer contribution strategy to make a one-off contribution of up to $300,000 each ($600,000 per couple) to your new superannuation account from the proceeds of the sale of your home.
soa.outcomesLine: The proceeds of your home sale are moved into the concessionally-taxed superannuation environment and used to fund a tax-free retirement income stream.
why: The downsizer contribution lets you move up to $300,000 each from the sale of a main residence (owned 10+ years, age 55+) into super, regardless of your other contribution caps or total super balance.
It allows the proceeds to be professionally managed in line with your risk profile and drawn as tax-free retirement income.
risks: There is the normal risk of markets falling and unforeseen circumstances requiring you to draw funds when markets are down.

By investing your cash into a superannuation fund instead of a bank account you lose capital stability and a known rate of return. You also lose access to the government guarantee on deposits up to $250,000.
Funds are preserved — you cannot access them until you meet a condition of release.
alternatives: Retain the proceeds in cash/term deposits — discounted as it forgoes the tax-effective superannuation environment and professional management.
Contribute via non-concessional contributions instead — discounted where the downsizer rules allow a larger contribution without using your NCC caps.

modules.trigger: Contributions reserving strategy (double concessional cap before age 67)
modules.scopeGate: Super contributions scoped; client under 67 with capacity

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend implementing a contributions reserving strategy within your SMSF by making concessional contributions totalling [2 × cap] prior to 30 June. The full amount will be contributed and claimed as a tax deduction, with [one cap] in the current financial year and [one cap] in July (next financial year). This allows use of both years' concessional caps before age 67, when work test rules may limit further contributions.
soa.outcomesLine: You bring forward and claim two years' worth of concessional caps in the current financial year, maximising the tax deduction and capital moved into super before the work test applies.
why: By maximising your concessional contribution caps across both financial years before age 67, you enhance tax efficiency by reducing personal taxable income and increasing capital within the superannuation environment before work test requirements may apply.
risks: The strategy relies on your accountant confirming eligibility and lodging the relevant ATO contribution-reserving forms; incorrect implementation can cause an excess concessional contribution.
The Fund must hold the reserved contribution and allocate it within the prescribed period.
alternatives: Make a single year's concessional contribution only — discounted as it forgoes the additional cap available before the work test applies.

modules.trigger: First Home Super Saver Scheme (FHSSS)
modules.scopeGate: Client(s) saving for a first home; eligible to make voluntary contributions
modules.figures: Voluntary contributions up to the FHSSS limit; salary-sacrifice amount

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you each utilise the First Home Super Saver Scheme (FHSSS) to assist with the purchase of your first property: make a lump-sum personal contribution before 30 June, commence salary sacrificing up to the annual limit, and continue making voluntary contributions each year. Once you are prepared to purchase, withdraw your voluntary contributions and associated earnings by requesting a determination through myGov followed by a release request.
soa.outcomesLine: You save for your deposit inside super at concessional tax rates, then release the funds (plus deemed earnings) to put toward your first home.
why: Voluntary contributions are taxed concessionally in super, and the released amount (including associated earnings) is taxed more favourably than ordinary income, helping you build your deposit faster.
risks: Funds are accessible only for an eligible first-home purchase; if you don't proceed, the contributions remain preserved in super.
Income/timing matters — salary sacrifice may interact with co-contribution eligibility, and the release requires a myGov determination then a release request.
alternatives: Save the deposit outside super — discounted as it forgoes the FHSSS tax concession.

modules.trigger: Salary packaging (employer-provided, e.g. health / PBI sector)
modules.scopeGate: Employer offers salary packaging (commonly health/charity/PBI employers)
modules.figures: Maximum annual packaging amount available from the employer

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you commence salary packaging your income to the maximum amount available to you (e.g. $9,010 p.a.).
soa.outcomesLine: Pre-tax income is diverted to packaged benefits, reducing your taxable income.
why: Salary packaging reduces your assessable income at your marginal tax rate without using your concessional contribution cap, improving your after-tax position.
risks: Availability depends on your employer and role; it ceases if you change employers.
It can interact with means-tested benefits; coordinate with any salary sacrifice so you do not exceed your concessional cap.
alternatives: Forgo packaging and use post-tax income — discounted as it forgoes the tax saving available through your employer.

modules.trigger: Carry-forward concessional contribution to offset CGT on an asset sale
modules.scopeGate: A capital gain is being realised (e.g. investment property sale) and unused concessional cap is available
modules.figures: Estimated capital gain; carry-forward concessional contribution; CGT before vs after

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you each make a once-off concessional contribution using the carry-forward rule in the year you realise the capital gain (e.g. $26,000 each), claiming it as a tax deduction to reduce your assessable capital gain.
soa.outcomesLine: The deduction reduces the tax payable on the sale (e.g. reducing the CGT liability from $41,000 to $33,000) while boosting your super.
why: Unused concessional cap from prior years can be 'carried forward' and used in a high-income year to shelter a capital gain, moving money into the concessionally-taxed super environment.
risks: Requires sufficient carry-forward cap room and a total super balance under the threshold; the contribution must be made in the same financial year as the gain.
Contributions are preserved until a condition of release is met.
alternatives: Invest the sale proceeds outside super — discounted as it forgoes the CGT-offset benefit; or use the non-concessional cap (no deduction).

modules.trigger: Notice of intent — claim a tax deduction on unclaimed personal contributions

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you submit a notice of intent to claim a tax deduction on any unclaimed personal contributions made this and the previous financial year.
why: Claiming the deduction converts after-tax contributions into concessional ones, reducing your taxable income.

modules.trigger: Arrange salary sacrifice with employer (switch post-tax to pre-tax)

soa.strategiesLine: We recommend you speak with your employer to switch your current post-tax contributions to pre-tax salary-sacrifice contributions.
why: Pre-tax (salary-sacrifice) contributions are taxed at 15% rather than your marginal rate.

modules.trigger: Division 293 tax note (high-income earners)

soa.strategiesLine: Note: as a higher-income earner you may be subject to Division 293 tax — an additional 15% on concessional contributions where your income plus contributions exceeds the threshold.

modules.trigger: Division 296 tax note (total super balance over $3m)

soa.strategiesLine: Note: Division 296 may apply an additional tax on earnings attributable to the portion of your total super balance above $3m.

modules.trigger: Levels of cover as per quotes
triggerPhrases: levels of cover as per quotes

soa.strategiesLine: Levels of cover as per the attached quotes.

why: Your full existing personal debt, partial existing/proposed investment debt, and any funeral and final expenses will be covered.
